query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: Homogeneous HEA nanoparticle formation in noble metal–based systems is governed by achieving a synchronized reduction (or vaporization) of the constituent metal precursors. If the reduction kinetics of all metal precursors are converged—so that they nucleate simultaneously—each growing particle incorporates the full complement of metal atoms, leading to a single-phase alloy. In contrast, when the reduction events are staggered, sequential nucleation occurs, resulting in phase separation or core–shell morphologies.
generation.material_initial_state: A mixture of noble metal precursors (e.g., Pd, Pt, Rh, Ir, Ru) in solution or as elemental powders/vapors ready for reduction or evaporation.
generation.intervention: Modify the synthesis protocol to adjust conditions (such as temperature profile, solvent/reductant composition, or timing of precursor introduction) so as to narrow the intrinsic differences in reduction kinetics among the metal precursors.
generation.conditions: The reaction is conducted under controlled temperature and chemical environment where all metal precursors have the opportunity to reduce (or evaporate) in a synchronized manner. This is compared to a baseline synthesis where precursors reduce (or vaporize) at their natural, disparate rates.
generation.structural_mediator: The nucleation front of the growing nanoparticle structure, which, when fed by a concurrently available pool of metal atoms, mediates uniform alloy incorporation.
generation.mechanism: Synchronization of reduction kinetics ensures that metal atoms are concurrently available during nucleation. This simultaneous atomic incorporation prevents any individual element from dominating early nucleation events (which could lead to phase segregation or core–shell structures) and thereby fosters a homogeneous, single-phase alloy across particles.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the modified synthesis conditions that synchronize reduction kinetics, the resulting nanoparticles will exhibit a uniform, homogeneous elemental distribution with single-phase alloy crystallinity. In contrast, under baseline conditions with unmodified reduction kinetics, one would observe phase separation or elemental segregation.
generation.baseline: Synthesis conducted under unaltered conditions where inherent differences in the reduction (or evaporation) rates of the metal precursors lead to sequential nucleation events.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for noble metal–based HEA systems where the precursor chemistries and reaction media allow for modulation of reduction kinetics. It may not apply to systems with extremely disparate thermodynamic properties or to processes (such as certain plasma routes) where other factors (e.g., nucleation temperature gaps) dominate the mixing behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise window of intervention parameters (e.g., temperature, reagent concentration, timing adjustments) that optimally synchronize reduction kinetics is not yet fully quantified, and interactions with other synthesis variables (such as stabilizer and solvent effects) remain to be thoroughly explored.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled comparison in which one synthesis batch is processed using standard conditions (baseline) and another using an intervention designed to synchronize reduction kinetics (for example, by adjusting precursor concentrations or injection timing to reduce differences in reduction rates). Use identical precursor ratios and overall reaction conditions except for the synchronization intervention.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess phase purity and crystallinity
STEM-EDX mapping to evaluate uniformity of elemental distribution
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to gauge particle morphology and size uniformity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles produced under the synchronization intervention do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in homogeneous single-phase alloy formation (i.e., if elemental distributions, phase purity, and morphologies are equivalent to or worse than the baseline sample), then the hypothesis is falsified.

When benchmarked against the commercial Pt/C and phase-separated nanocrystals, the obtained PtPdRhIrRu HEA nanocrystals have high catalytic activity and durability toward electrocatalytic HER and HOR.
## One-pot synthesis of phase-separated multimetallic nanocrystals
We first conducted the one-pot synthesis to examine whether the one-shot injection of the precursor solution instead of dropwise addition would obtain solid-solution HEA nanocrystals. Because of the different reduction kinetics of metal precursors and thus sequential generations of atoms, it is expected that the one-pot synthesis will induce the formation of phase-separated nanocrystals.
